title: Gravitational potential and energy; Stellar spectra, HR diagram and stellar evolution
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: A02-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; A02-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; C04-uk1#t1 term and clue written for the game; C04-uk1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: A02-1#N.2, A02-1#N.12, A02-1#N.13, A02-1#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Protostar
items.clue: Cloud of dust and gas heating up as it collapses under gravity.

items.label: White dwarf
items.clue: Hot, dim, tiny object with no fusion, at the lower left of the HR diagram.

items.label: Gravitational potential
items.clue: Quantity V outside a planet: negative, varying as 1/r and rising to zero far away.

items.label: Gravitational field strength
items.clue: Quantity g outside a planet, varying as 1/r²: a quarter of its surface value at 2R.

questions.stem: Suppose the rate of fusion in a main-sequence star's core suddenly fell. What would happen to the core at first?

options.text: It would expand, because less energy is being released inside it.
It would contract: the pressure would fall, so gravity would no longer be balanced.
Nothing would change, because the star's rotation balances its gravity.
It would explode, because the forces on it would no longer be balanced.

questions.explanation: Fusion keeps the core hot, which maintains the gas and radiation pressure. With less pressure, inward gravity wins and the core contracts (and heats up as it does).

questions.stem: Astronomers observe a glowing shell of gas expanding gently away from a very hot, very small star at its centre: a planetary nebula. Which describes the central star?

options.text: It was a red giant of low mass; it will now slowly cool and fade as a white dwarf.
It was a red supergiant; it will soon explode as a supernova and leave a neutron star.
It is a protostar forming from the gas; it will soon join the main sequence.
It is a neutron star left by a supernova; it will later collapse into a black hole.

questions.explanation: A planetary nebula is the outer layers of a low-mass red giant drifting off. The exposed hot core is a white dwarf: no fusion, so it cools and fades.

questions.stem: After a star's supernova, the core left behind has a mass of 1.7 times the Sun's mass. What does the core become?

options.text: A white dwarf, held up by electron degeneracy pressure
A neutron star, because it is above the Chandrasekhar limit
A black hole, because every core above the Chandrasekhar limit becomes one
A red giant, because the core starts fusing hydrogen again

questions.explanation: Above about 1.4 solar masses the core collapses past the white-dwarf stage. At this mass it stops as a neutron star.

questions.stem: Astronomers find a neutron star at the centre of the expanding remains of a supernova. What can be concluded about the star that produced it, compared with the Sun?

options.text: It had about the Sun's mass, and its red giant stage ended in a supernova.
It had far more mass than the Sun, and a shorter main-sequence life.
It had far more mass than the Sun, and a longer main-sequence life.
It had less mass than the Sun, and collapsed as soon as its fusion stopped.

questions.explanation: Only massive stars end in a supernova that leaves a neutron star. More mass means much faster fusion, so the star leaves the main sequence much sooner.
